questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Steps for Problem Solving' refers to.
questions.a: Solving a task on a computer runs through four stages: analyse the statement to pin down inputs and outputs, draft an algorithm, translate it into a program (coding), then test and debug until every kind of input yields the right output.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Steps for Problem Solving'.
questions.a: Garbage in, garbage out: a wrong input analysis poisons every later stage of the solution.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Steps for Problem Solving', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle

questions.q: Using the method 'Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle', work with: breadth = 25, length = 45. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of perim.
Take the relation taught for 'Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle' and work with: breadth = 75, length = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of perim.
Explain in your own words what 'Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle' refers to.
questions.a: A first algorithm records its input, states the processing and names the output; for a rectangle the processing multiplies length by breadth for area, and doubles the sum of the sides for perimeter.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle'.
questions.a: Every algorithm should begin by fixing three things: the input accepted, the processing done, and the output printed.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Average of Five Numbers with a Counter Loop

questions.q: Using the method 'Average of Five Numbers with a Counter Loop', work with: n1 = 240, n2 = 240, n3 = 45, n4 = 120, n5 = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of average.

Take the relation taught for 'Average of Five Numbers with a Counter Loop' and work with: n1 = 120, n2 = 500, n3 = 300, n4 = 400, n5 = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of average.
Explain in your own words what 'Average of Five Numbers with a Counter Loop' refers to.
questions.a: A counting loop reads one number per pass, adds it to a running total, and bumps a counter; when the counter reaches the loop limit, the total divided by the count of values gives the average.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Average of Five Numbers with a Counter Loop'.
questions.a: The counter both decides when the loop ends and records how many values entered the total.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Average of Five Numbers with a Counter Loop', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Selection with Conditionals: Even or Odd

questions.q: Using the method 'Selection with Conditionals: Even or Odd', work with: number = 4096. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of even_check.
Take the relation taught for 'Selection with Conditionals: Even or Odd' and work with: number = 4096. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of even_check.
Explain in your own words what 'Selection with Conditionals: Even or Odd' refers to.
questions.a: Selection lets an algorithm pick between two paths by testing a condition that evaluates to true or false; testing the remainder on division by 2 routes a number to the even or the odd branch.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Selection with Conditionals: Even or Odd'.
questions.a: A zero remainder after dividing by 2 signals an even number; anything else signals odd.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Selection with Conditionals: Even or Odd', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Dry Run of a Time-Adding Algorithm

questions.q: Using the method 'Dry Run of a Time-Adding Algorithm', work with: hh1 = 150, hh2 = 150, mm1 = 80, mm2 = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_hours.
Take the relation taught for 'Dry Run of a Time-Adding Algorithm' and work with: hh1 = 400, hh2 = 8, mm1 = 12, mm2 = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_hours.
Explain in your own words what 'Dry Run of a Time-Adding Algorithm' refers to.
questions.a: Verifying an algorithm means walking through its steps with sample inputs, called a dry run; adding two durations exposes a missing carry when the minutes cross 60, which the corrected algorithm folds into the hours.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Dry Run of a Time-Adding Algorithm'.
questions.a: A dry run with a case that crosses the boundary, such as 70 minutes, is what reveals a missing carry step.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Dry Run of a Time-Adding Algorithm', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Sum of First N Natural Numbers

questions.q: Using the method 'Sum of First N Natural Numbers', work with: n = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total.
Take the relation taught for 'Sum of First N Natural Numbers' and work with: n = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total.
Explain in your own words what 'Sum of First N Natural Numbers' refers to.
questions.a: The total of the numbers from 1 to N has a closed form: multiply N by N plus one and halve the product; small cases such as N equals 6 give 21, which is how the formula is verified by hand.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sum of First N Natural Numbers'.
questions.a: Checking a formula against small manually computed cases is the simplest way to verify it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sum of First N Natural Numbers', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Prime Testing and Algorithm Complexity', work with: number = 4096. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of checks_saved.
Take the relation taught for 'Prime Testing and Algorithm Complexity' and work with: number = 256. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of checks_saved.
Explain in your own words what 'Prime Testing and Algorithm Complexity' refers to.
questions.a: A prime check can test divisors up to the number, up to half of it, or only up to its square root; each refinement cuts the divisibility trials, which is exactly the trade-off captured by time complexity and, when a prime list is stored, space complexity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Prime Testing and Algorithm Complexity'.
questions.a: Two algorithms that agree on the answer can still differ hugely in processing time and memory use.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Prime Testing and Algorithm Complexity', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Decomposition of Complex Problems' refers to.
questions.a: Decomposition splits a complex job, like a railway reservation system, into smaller sub-problems that can be solved and tested separately, often by different teams, and then joined into one working whole.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Decomposition of Complex Problems'.
questions.a: Divide and conquer: each sub-problem is easier than the original and can be assigned to specialist teams.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Decomposition of Complex Problems', in plain ASCII form.
